article.headline: Charcuterie Maps Unicode's 160,000 Characters by Visual Shape
article.lede: Unicode 17.0 defines nearly 160,000 assigned characters — each catalogued by name, script, block, and codepoint. Every existing browser for the standard organizes them by that taxonomy, which is useful for engineers but maddening for anyone who knows what a character looks like but cannot name it. Charcuterie, built by Zürich-based interaction developer David Aerne, inverts the interface: choose a glyph, and the tool returns everything in the standard that looks like it.
article.body:
The application offers three ways in. The first is conventional: browse by script or block category via dropdown. The second is a text search by character name. The third — the one that drew attention when Aerne announced the project in April 2026 — is a sketch mode in which the user draws a shape with the cursor and the tool returns the closest matching glyphs. Aerne himself called the feature rough (“pretty badly for now”), but the underlying engine makes even an imprecise stroke productive. The name is a deliberate pun: a *charcuterie* board assembles odd cuts from many sources into one coherent spread; the tool does the same for Unicode's heterogeneous catalog of scripts, symbols, punctuation, emoji, and obscure dingbats.

The technical pipeline is straightforward in concept and unusual in application. Every Unicode character is rasterized — rendered to a pixel bitmap in a standard font — and then passed through **CLIP** (Contrastive Language–Image Pretraining), a vision-language encoder developed by OpenAI and released in 2021. Trained on hundreds of millions of image-text pairs scraped from the web, CLIP learns to project images and text into a shared *vector space* so that visually or semantically related items cluster together. When Aerne feeds it *glyph* bitmaps, the model carries no specific knowledge of typography — but it has absorbed enough visual information to understand that a cedilla under a C resembles a hook under a Q, that circled digits belong apart from squared ones, that ornamental flourishes cluster regardless of which script they dress. At query time, a *nearest-neighbor search* retrieves the characters whose CLIP embeddings sit closest to the query. Everything runs client-side in the browser; no query leaves the device.

Aerne, who operates under the studio name Elastiq GmbH, has built his open-source reputation almost entirely around navigation systems for aesthetic spaces. His most-starred project, **color-names**, is a curated lexicon of nearly 32,000 unique color names distributed as JSON, CSV, and a free REST API — a tool for giving human language to the RGB color cube's 16 million addressable values. Companion projects *poline* and *rampensau* generate harmonious palettes via polar-coordinate and hue-cycling algorithms respectively. Charcuterie follows the same underlying thesis: a very large, formally-structured space made navigable through sensory intuition rather than lookup.

A caveat worth filing: **Unicode does not define visual shapes.** The standard assigns names, properties, and encoded values to characters — but not how they are drawn. That is the job of fonts and rendering engines. Charcuterie's similarity judgments are therefore judgments about a specific rasterization: a character that resembles an arrow in Aerne's chosen rendering may look nothing like one in a different typeface. The tool is, more precisely, a glyph-similarity explorer for one particular rendering of the Unicode codespace, addressed through Unicode's numbering scheme. That caveat does not diminish its usefulness for designers and typographers working in a standard rendering environment — it simply means the “visual similarity” is not an intrinsic property of the codepoints themselves.

concepts.definition: CLIP (Contrastive Language–Image Pretraining) is a vision-language encoder developed by OpenAI that maps both images and text into a shared high-dimensional space so that visually or semantically related items cluster together. When two images are similar, their CLIP vectors are close; when they are unrelated, the vectors are distant. Charcuterie uses CLIP to embed rendered glyph images so that visually similar Unicode characters end up near each other and can be retrieved by proximity.

A mathematical structure in which each item is represented as an ordered list of numbers (a vector). Distance between vectors encodes similarity: items whose vectors are close share properties that the model learned to encode. Machine learning systems like CLIP project images into high-dimensional vector spaces so that similarity can be computed and searched efficiently at scale.

A computational method for finding the k items in a dataset whose vectors are closest to a query vector, typically measured by cosine or Euclidean distance. In Charcuterie, it retrieves the Unicode characters whose CLIP embeddings most closely match the query glyph's embedding, producing the visual-similarity results the user sees.

The visual form of a character as rendered by a specific font in a specific context. A single Unicode codepoint can produce many different glyphs depending on typeface, weight, and rendering engine. Charcuterie works with glyphs — specific pixel renderings — rather than abstract codepoints, which is why its similarity results are tied to the font used to generate the embeddings.

The process of converting a vector-based description, such as a font outline, into a grid of pixels (a bitmap). Charcuterie rasterizes each Unicode character — renders it to a fixed-size pixel image — before passing it to the CLIP encoder to generate an embedding vector.

A unique integer assigned to each character in the Unicode standard, written conventionally as U+XXXX in hexadecimal (e.g., U+0041 for the Latin capital letter A). Codepoints are abstract addresses; they specify identity and properties but say nothing about visual appearance, which is delegated to fonts and rendering engines.

A contiguous range of codepoints in the Unicode standard assigned to a related group of characters — for example, “Basic Latin,” “Dingbats,” or “CJK Unified Ideographs.” Blocks are the primary organizational axis of conventional Unicode browsers, grouping characters by script or functional category rather than by appearance.

repos.summary: A curated collection of nearly 32,000 unique color names mapped to hex values, distributed as JSON, CSV, YAML, and an npm package with a free REST API. It covers an evenly distributed sample of the RGB color space and gives human-readable names to otherwise anonymous hex codes. Used by design tools, accessibility checkers, and creative coding projects worldwide.

A palette generator that interpolates between color anchor points using polar coordinates in HSL space, tracing arc-shaped paths rather than straight lines through the color solid. The technique avoids the muddy midpoints common in naive linear RGB interpolation. Used by designers and generative artists who want mathematically coherent color progressions.

A color palette generation library that produces ramps by cycling through hue ranges with configurable easing curves and control over saturation and lightness progressions. Useful for generating perceptually balanced color scales for data visualization and UI design. Part of Aerne's consistent body of work building principled navigational tools for color space.
